the elucidation of the role of estrogen deficiency, cytokines, PTH and vitamin D in the genesis of bone loss associated with aging.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

estrogen is the most important factor in the regulation of bone turnover in both young and old women, and that estrogen deficiency in menopausal women causes an increase in bone resorption, which is probably mediated by immune system cytokines.
the endocrine system is the main determinant of the osteoporotic process, although the precise mechanism by which the various hormones exert their effects on bone remains to be elucidated.
the endocrine system plays a key role in the pathophysiology of postmenopausal bone loss.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the bone-protective effects of estrogen are exerted by the suppression of the biosynthesis of immune system cytokine by osteoblast.
the endocrine system plays an important role in the pathogenesis of osteoporosis, but it is not the only system involved.
the osteoporosis of menopause is a complex disease in which estrogen deficiency plays an important, but not exclusive, role.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the osteoporosis occurring in early menopausal women is caused by the loss of the suppressive effects of estrogen on the immune system and that this loss is responsible for the release of cytokines which stimulate bone destruction.
the bone-protective effects of estrogens are not due to the inhibition of osteoclasts, but to the stimulation of osteoblasts.

the endocrine changes associated with aging are not limited to the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, but involve also the hypothalamic pituitary-thyroid and -parathyroid axes and the immune system, which are all interrelated.
